newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS - EU set to agree Cr.Lyonnais emergency aid.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - EU set to agree Cr.Lyonnais emergency aid.

text.p: The European Commission was set on Wednesday to approve emergency aid of about 4 billion francs ($785 million) for embattled French state-owned bank Credit Lyonnais, European Union sources said.

One source said the EU executive was also expected to open a probe into planned changes of a restructuring plan which was approved last year although the French government had not yet made any formal proposals.
"(The Commission) must open a procedure for a number of reasons," the source said.
EU Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert was expected to annouce the decision at a new conference in Brussels at 1015 GMT.

The EU source said the Commission had been asked to approve the proposed emergency aid. "The Commission has in a sense got to do what is proposed...The rescue (aid) will be approved," the source said.

Another EU source confirmed that the Commission was expected to clear the emergency aid but that the amount of approved aid could be less than four billion francs and that it was not certain that the Commission would decide to open a state aid probe.
"As far as I understand, France is not proposing now to change the 1995 plan. It will come back with the changes before the end of the year," this source said.
France informed the Commission only on Tuesday night of its plan to grant further aid to the troubled bank.
French business daily La Tribune earlier on Wednesday said the French government hopes to get the green light from the Commission for an emergency state aid of 3.9 billion francs.
The newspaper said the aid for which Paris was seeking clearance was emergency aid only and could be followed up by a new rescue package.

Sources close to the talks had raised the possibility of a new rescue plan involving a 10-billion-franc recapitalisation, the paper said, adding that Lyonnais chairman Jean Peyrelevade met Van Miert on Tuesday.

Credit Lyonnais, once the largest bank outside of Japan, is being restructured under the 1995 plan allowing for maximum 45 billion French francs in subsidies. It has become clear, however, that a new plan will have to be drafted if the bank is to avoid slipping again into the red.
